newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany warn its troops to be vigilant in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Germany warn its troops to be vigilant in Bosnia.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe, inspecting troops that will join a new Bosnia peacekeeping force, on Thursday urged the soldiers to be vigilant on their historic mission.

At this fog-shrouded army base 100 kilometres (60 miles) east of Frankfurt, Ruehe paid a morale-boosting visit to Bundeswehr soldiers training to be part of the first German combat units deployed abroad since World War Two.
About 3,300 German soldiers will join the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in January in Bosnia, where memories of atrocities committed by Hitler's armies are still alive.

The German force will include 2,000 infantry and armoured vehicle-borne reconnaissance troops equipped for combat. It is a deployment that until recently would have been unthinkable in a country deeply scarred by its Nazi past.
"They have the full support of parliament and the population and that is very important for the soldiers," said Ruehe, who tramped through mud and drizzle to talk with the troops for several hours.
"I told them they shouldn't feel too secure there at any time," Ruehe said. "Nothing should become routine. They will need their utmost concentration every hour of every day."
With backing from Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Ruehe has whittled away strong pacificist sentiment left behind by Germany's ignominious militaristic past.

Step-by-step efforts to remove the taboo on German troops being deployed abroad began in 1992, with manpower and equipment sent to a field hospital in Cambodia, and culminated in a vote a year ago to send 4,000 troops to the IFOR mission that preceded SFOR.

But the government limited the Bundeswehr's role in IFOR to logistics tasks such as bridge-building because of concerns German troops would revive memories of the Nazi occupation of Yugoslavia and brutal repression during World War Two.
To avoid any possible confrontation with the Serbs, German troops were also stationed only in Croatia, rather than Bosnia.

The German soldiers have earned praise. In the 18-month SFOR mission starting in January they will for the first time be full partners in the peacekeeping alongside troops from the U.S., France and Britain.
"The Bundeswehr has proven itself," Ruehe said.
The combat deployment to Bosnia, which has attracted remarkably little dissent in Germany, was beyond the imagination of even the army's strongest backers a year ago.
Even Ruehe stated German troops would "not under any circumstances" be sent to Bosnia.
"We are going there because we are part of the solution, not part of the problem," Ruehe said when asked about his changed stance.

The combat deployment also marks a dramatic about-face for Germany since the 1991 Gulf War, when Germany paid a staggering $5.5 billion to the multinational force that drove Iraq from Kuwait rather than send even a token force of soldiers.
